question: Should social networks attach warning labels to false posts rather than delete them?
answer: Labels inform without silencing. Experiments find fact-check tags cut belief in, and sharing of, flagged claims, and corrections rarely backfire. Deletion hands the author a censorship story, pushes followers to platforms no correction reaches, and makes a company the judge of truth. A label keeps the false post and its rebuttal side by side.
move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is what happens to the posts nobody checks.
ask: When something I see online carries no warning, do I treat that as a sign it has been checked?
counterpoint: Labels arrive late and leak. Pennycook and colleagues found an implied truth effect: once some false headlines carried warnings, unlabelled false ones were believed more, as if checked. Fact-checkers can tag only a sliver of what spreads, and corrected beliefs tend to drift back within weeks. For harmful falsehoods, removal stops the spread at its source.
source: Pennycook, Bear, Collins & Rand, Management Science, 2020
reference: Pennycook, Bear, Collins & Rand, The implied truth effect: attaching warnings to a subset of fake news headlines increases perceived accuracy of headlines without warnings, Management Science, 2020
